$schema-note: Hand-maintained. Data, not code: nothing in domain/, application/ or contracts/ imports this file.
purpose: The guard ledger for WIN-259 (M2.4) — redaction, write-only inputs, the
removal of raw-secret response paths, and audit events for secret access.
One entry per guard, each carrying the file it lives in, the EXACT text that
implements it (`from`), the edit that removes it (`to`), and the NAMED cases
that were seen to go red (`kills`).
PATHS ARE RELATIVE TO THE REPOSITORY ROOT, not to this package, and that is
the one thing about this ledger that differs from every other one in the
tree. The guards this issue adds deliberately span four projects — the
kernel declares the redaction the Logger port promises, the composition root
applies it, `secrets` owns the write-only boundary and the audit trail, and
`providers` is the one peer that hands `secrets` material. A projection
boundary that lived in one package would not BE a boundary. It lives here
rather than in packages/kernel because `secrets` is the context WIN-259 is
about and because the kernel may hold no data file of its own under
procedure: For one entry: replace its `from` with its `to` in the named file, rebuild
what the named suites read (see `rebuild`), run those suites, and confirm a
NAMED case goes red. Then revert and confirm green. A mutation that leaves
every case green is a finding, not a pass.
REBUILD MATTERS HERE AND IT IS EASY TO GET A VACUOUS KILL WITHOUT IT. A
suite inside a package reads that package's SOURCE through vite; a suite in
another package reads the first package's `dist`. So mutating
packages/kernel and running apps/core-api's suite proves nothing until
`tsc -b packages/kernel` has run, and mutating packages/contexts/secrets and
has. Each entry names what to rebuild.
TWO ENTRIES RECORD A LIMIT RATHER THAN A GUARD, and they are declared with a
MEASURED reason instead of a kill that was not got. Both are in the
`unfalsifiable` list at the end. Counting them as kills would have been the
easier and less useful thing to write down.

unfalsifiable.name: M29 denied audit: the PLAIN-variable guard in recordDeniedVariableRead
reason: MEASURED, not assumed. The guard refuses to record a denial for a
variable that has no backing credential. Removing it does not change
the outcome, because `recordDeniedRead` beneath it resolves the
credential and returns without writing when none is found. Both
paths therefore produce an identical audit trail and an identical
answer, and `records NOTHING for a refused PLAIN variable read`
stays green either way.
What distinguishes them is WHERE the refusal happens: with the guard
the credential store is never touched, without it a lookup is spent
on a row that cannot exist. Telling those apart needs a call counter
on the in-memory credential store, which this branch did not add —
the guard is cheap and correct, and inventing a counter to make one
line falsifiable would have been a test written for the ledger
rather than for the system.
IT IS KEPT ANYWAY, and the reason is the same one that makes it hard
to falsify: it states the intent at the point a reader asks the
question, one frame before the answer arrives by accident.

unfalsifiable.name: M30 denied audit: the minted check in recordDeniedVariableRead
reason: MEASURED. The same shape as M29 one frame up. `recordDeniedRead`
checks minted-ness itself, so removing this copy leaves the audit
trail and the caller's answer identical and `records NOTHING for an
unminted authorization` stays green.
The difference is again a store read: the lookup this guard sits in
front of is keyed on `authorization.environmentId`, and on a forged
literal that field is whatever the forger typed. Without the check a
caller with no grant at all can make this process read a variable
row at an address it chose. Nothing observable comes back, so no
assertion about the RESULT can see the difference; seeing it needs a
store call counter, for the reason M29 gives.

unfalsifiable.name: M35 census: a has*/is* presence-prefix filter — DELETED rather than declared
reason: This one is here because it is the opposite of the two above: the
sweep could not turn it red, and the right answer was to DELETE it
rather than to declare it.
`MATERIAL_RESPONSE_KEYS` is a closed list and `hasClientSecret` is
not in it, so no input could reach the prefix filter that the list
had not already refused. It read like a guard, it was tested by a
case that passed without it, and it was doing nothing. A guard
nothing can falsify is a comment, so it is one now — the prose above
the key list says which names look material and are not.
The case that covered it is KEPT and its reason rewritten, because
the PROPERTY is still true and still worth pinning; only the claim
about which code provides it has changed.

unfalsifiable.name: M53 reference: the credential-resolves guard in recordDeniedExchange
reason: MEASURED, not assumed, and it is the third of this shape after M29 and
M30. The guard refuses to write a denial row for a reference whose
credential does not resolve in the presented grant's environment.
IT CANNOT BE REMOVED AND MEASURED. `findCredential` answers
`CredentialWithActiveVersion | null`, so deleting the null arm does not
produce a program that runs and answers differently -- it produces one
that does not compile, and a type error is not a measurement. Rewriting
it to force a non-null would be measuring a mutation nobody could
plausibly write.
WHAT STANDS IN ITS PLACE IS A DATABASE, AND THAT IS THE STRONGER
EVIDENCE. `an audit row naming a credential from ANOTHER environment is
refused by the database`, in
packages/adapters/postgres-tenancy/src/secrets-rules.integration.test.ts,
shows what the absence would cost:
`CredentialAudit_credentialId_environmentId_fkey` raises mid-transaction
and takes the exchange down with it. The guard turns a poisoned
transaction into a deliberate silence; the composite key -- which is in
the MIGRATION and in neither `schema.prisma`'s generated types nor any
port signature -- is what makes the alternative loud. `inMemorySecretsStore`
keys its audit rows by nothing and would have accepted the pair, so all
26 exchange cases pass either way and only PostgreSQL can say this.

result: 49 entries. ALL 49 killed by a NAMED case, and 4 more declared in
`unfalsifiable` above -- three guards kept with a measured reason why no
assertion about the result can see them, and one guard DELETED because the
sweep proved it was dead.
M23 IS THE ENTRY TO READ FIRST. On the first pass it was the one entry with
no kill of its own, recorded as a COMPOUND measurement: it changed nothing
alone and was the mechanism by which M21 and M22 were killed. An integrator
counted 37 entries against 36 named kills and held the branch back for it,
and it was right to: a ledger whose own rule is one entry one kill has to
meet it or say why. The repair was to WRITE THE CASE rather than to declare
the gap -- three cases now drive the vault double directly, the acceptance
half minting its material with the one mint `secrets` publishes so the
double is held to the real vault rather than to a shape this package owns.
M23 is now KILLED, and its compound history is kept beside the kills
because the history is the finding.
NONE OF THE KILLS IS VACUOUS. Every one names a case that was seen red and
green, and the `rebuild` field on each entry is what keeps a cross-package
kill honest: `providers` reads `secrets` through dist, so M21 and M22 would
have reported a kill they had not got if the sweep had not rebuilt.
THE SWEEP CHANGED THE CODE THREE TIMES ON THE FIRST PASS, which is the point
of running it. M35's guard was deleted as dead. M29 and M30 moved from
claimed to declared. And three census drift rules (M37, M39, M40) SURVIVED
their first removal -- `check()` read the committed manifest off disk, so its
four drift rules were all silent by construction and a suite could only
assert that nothing was wrong. `check()` now takes a substituted manifest,
and six cases exercise the rules that a green repository can never reach.
THE SECOND PASS ADDED TWELVE (M41-M52) FOR THE SECRET REFERENCE, and two of
them are worth naming because they are not deleted guards. M41 does not
disable a comparison -- there is no comparison to disable; it takes the
environment out of the key derivation and the AAD, and the two environments
then derive the same keystream and the same tag. M51 mutates the in-memory
CIPHER rather than the code under test, because every reference case is
proved against that authenticator and a double that stopped checking its tag
would make the environment-binding and tamper cases pass against nothing.
AND ONE MORE WAS DECLARED RATHER THAN COUNTED. M53's guard cannot be removed
and measured -- deleting it produces a type error and not a program -- so it
is declared, and the evidence standing in for it is a real PostgreSQL
composite foreign key that the in-memory store does not have.
